The Seventh Victim is a 1943 American horror film directed by Mark Robson and starring Tom Conway, Jean Brooks, Isabel Jewell, and Kim Hunter in her film debut. Written by Charles O'Neal and DeWitt Bodeen, and produced by Val Lewton for RKO Radio Pictures, the film focuses on a young woman who stumbles on an underground cult of devil worshippers in Greenwich Village, New York City, while searching for her missing sister.

The story The Seventh Victim tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. O'Neal had written the script as a murder mystery, set in California, that followed a woman hunted by a serial killer. Bodeen revised the script, basing the story on a Satanic society meeting he attended in New York City and setting it as a prequel to Cat People (1942), with Conway reprising his role as Dr.

Meaning is not found in The Seventh Victim — it is manufactured for it. Filming took place over 24 days in May 1943 at RKO Studios in Los Angeles. Released on August 21, 1943, the film failed to garner significant income at the box office and received mixed reviews from critics, who found its narrative incoherence a primary fault.

The cold light on The Seventh Victim leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. It was later revealed that Robson and editor John Lockert had removed four substantial scenes from the final cut, including an extended conclusion. In spite of its mixed reception, it became a cult film in England, noted by critics for its homoerotic undertones.

The Seventh Victim did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. Mary Gibson, a young woman at Highcliffe Academy, a boarding school, is informed by the principal that her older sister and only relative, Jacqueline, has gone missing and has not paid Mary's tuition in months. Mary decides to leave the school to find her sister, who owns La Sagesse, a cosmetics company in New York City.

The honest version of The Seventh Victim starts by giving up the comforting part. Upon arriving in New York, Mary meets Esther Redi at the cosmetics company, who had been Jacqueline's assistant, and she tells Mary that Jacqueline sold the business to her eight months earlier. Jacqueline's close friend and La Sagesse employee, Frances Fallon, claims to have seen Jacqueline the week before at Dante, an Italian restaurant in Greenwich Village.

Strip The Seventh Victim of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. Mary soon discovers that Jacqueline has rented a room above Dante, without having moved in. Mary persuades the owners to let her see the room, which she finds empty aside from a wooden chair and a noose hanging from the ceiling.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — The Seventh Victim shows exactly where that breaks. While at Dante, Mary meets Jason Hoag, a frustrated poet, who offers to help find her sister. Mary's investigation leads her to several individuals who knew Jacqueline, including her secret husband, attorney Gregory Ward, and a psychiatrist, Dr.

What looks like free choice in The Seventh Victim is older than choice itself. Mary learns Jacqueline had been a patient of Judd's, seeking treatment for depression stemming from her membership in a Satanic cult called the Palladists, and her subsequent efforts to leave the group. Jacqueline was lured into joining the cult by her former co-workers at La Sagesse, particularly Esther.

Nobody designed the part of The Seventh Victim you experience — it was inherited. When Mary and Irving break into La Sagesse after hours, Irving is stabbed to death by an unseen assailant. Mary flees into the subway, where she witnesses two men board her car, carrying Irving's corpse between them.

Every serious account of The Seventh Victim eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. She attempts to alert the police, but the men vanish with Irving's body before they arrive. Judd offers to bring Mary to visit Jacqueline at his residence, where she has been in hiding.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of The Seventh Victim — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. There, Mary is briefly met by Jacqueline, who gestures her to be quiet before again vanishing. Determined to remain in New York, Mary takes a job at a kindergarten.

The selfish-gene reading of The Seventh Victim makes it less romantic and far more precise. Some time later, Esther breaks into Mary's apartment and confronts her in the shower, claiming that Jacqueline murdered Irving and urging Mary to return to Highcliffe. Mary tells Gregory and Jason what Esther told her and they resolve to locate Jacqueline.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. Believing that murder is permissible only as a last resort, the Paladists prefer to goad perceived offenders into committing suicide. Frances, because of her attachment to Jacqueline, begs the cult members to spare her, to no avail.

The feeling that The Seventh Victim means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. The cultists kidnap Jacqueline and, over several hours, harangue her to drink from a glass of poison placed before her. When her will breaks and she reaches for the glass, Frances swipes the glass out of Jacqueline's hand and to the floor.

Nothing in The Seventh Victim was built for you — it was built for reproduction. The Palladists let Jacqueline leave, but they send an assassin to follow her. The assassin chases her through the streets with a switchblade, but she eludes him and returns to her rented room above Dante.

The psychology underneath The Seventh Victim is simpler and older than the story on top. In the rooming house hallway, Jacqueline briefly encounters her neighbor, Mimi, a terminally ill young woman. Mimi confesses to Jacqueline that she is afraid to die, and plans to have one last night out on the town.

Behind The Seventh Victim sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. Jacqueline enters her own apartment and apparently hangs herself; Mimi hears the thud of the chair falling over as she leaves for the evening. Most controversially, the film resolves with the suicide of one of the main characters (contrary to the spirit if not the letter of the Production Code).

The nihilist does not deny The Seventh Victim — he only refuses to flatter it. Film historian Steve Haberman, in his audio commentary for the 2005 Warner Bros. Critics have noted homosexual undercurrents running through the film, particularly in Jacqueline's character and her relationship with Frances, a cult member who is an employee at the company she formerly owned.

What culture calls destiny in The Seventh Victim is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. The film was featured in Turner Classic Movies' Screened Out, which celebrated gay and lesbian themes in classical Hollywood cinema. Benshoff, author of Monsters in the Closet: Homosexuality and the Horror Film (1997), have read the film's anchoring of its Palladist characters in Greenwich Village—a neighborhood with a history of gay and lesbian residents—as another prominent undercurrent.

The genes do not care about The Seventh Victim; they care about copies. The script for The Seventh Victim went through several incarnations in the pre-production process. One version focused on an orphan caught in a murder plot amid California's Signal Hill oil wells; in this narrative, the heroine needed to solve the orphan's identity, saving him from becoming the seventh victim of the unknown killer.

Take away the meaning and The Seventh Victim still functions — that is the disturbing part. This version of the script was re-written entirely by DeWitt Bodeen under the supervision of producer Val Lewton. The new plot followed a young woman who uncovers a cult of Satanists in Greenwich Village.

The unconscious does not argue with The Seventh Victim; it simply acts first. Bodeen purportedly based his idea for the film on a real Satanic society he had encountered in New York. The script incorporated other elements of his experiences in New York: Jacqueline's cosmetics business, La Sagesse, was inspired by his previous work as a journalist reporting on cosmetic companies, and the Italian restaurant, Dante, was based on Barbetta, a restaurant in Manhattan's Theater District.

The Seventh Victim feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. Jacques Tourneur, who had previously directed a trio of horror films for Lewton at RKO—Cat People, I Walked with a Zombie, and The Leopard Man—was originally slated to direct The Seventh Victim. However, Mark Robson, a Canadian editor who had worked as an assistant on Citizen Kane, was signed to direct instead, marking his directorial debut.

The bleak reading of The Seventh Victim is also the most testable one. It was shot over 24 days at RKO's Gower Street studio in Los Angeles, from May 5 to 29, 1943. The opening scene at the boarding school used the set featured in RKO's The Magnificent Ambersons, released the year before.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about The Seventh Victim. Mark Robson and John Lockert made multiple edits to the film during post-production, according to Lewton and Bodeen, resulting in a slightly "disjointed" narrative. Much of the confusion in The Seventh Victim would have been eliminated if scenes weren't cut.

The self that experiences The Seventh Victim is a committee, not a king. There was a final scene, after the woman hanged herself, that was just a horrible rehash, and it was wisely cut. It's a great ending, with the final scene taken out, but that last shot (when we hear the chair fall) needs to hold for another four or five seconds, just enough time to let it sink in.

Reproduction explains more of The Seventh Victim than any philosophy dares to admit. The movie just ends, and the reason was because they couldn't go back to reshoot it. A second excised scene features Judd visiting Natalie Cortez, pretending to be interested in joining the Palladists.
